claims.text: The solutionized equiatomic or near-equiatomic Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr baseline is a single-phase BCC alloy.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy typically has room-temperature yield strength above 1200 MPa.
The baseline alloy typically has less than 2% room-temperature ductility.
The poor room-temperature ductility of the baseline is caused by brittle cleavage.
The baseline alloy has a density above 12 g/cm³ because of its Hf and Ta content.
Substitution with 5–10 at% V followed by solutionizing at 1400°C and aging at 800°C for 10 hours will induce nanoscale precipitation.
The induced precipitates will be coherent or semi-coherent B2-ordered (Hf,Mo,Ta,Ti,Zr,V) nanoclusters in a BCC matrix.
B2 nanoclusters will strengthen the alloy by obstructing dislocation motion through cutting or bypass processes.
V-enriched BCC matrix regions will have enhanced stacking-fault energy and reduced Peierls stress.
Reduced Peierls stress from V addition will promote cross-slip, dislocation multiplication, and plastic flow before fracture.
V addition and the proposed dual-phase microstructure will suppress brittle cleavage and improve room-temperature ductility.
Replacing part of the heavier Hf and Ta content with V will reduce bulk density.
The modified alloy will have yield strength above 1000 MPa.
The modified alloy will have room-temperature tensile elongation above 10%.
The modified alloy will have a density 5–8% below that of the baseline.
Vacuum or inert-argon processing is necessary to prevent oxidation.
Aging must remain between 750°C and 850°C to preserve precipitate coherency and avoid over-aging.
V content must remain below approximately 15 at% to avoid formation of a continuous brittle network.
Aging beyond 24 hours will cause precipitate coarsening and degradation of strength.
V addition may stabilize brittle sigma or Laves phases instead of the desired B2 phase, eliminating the expected ductility benefit.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says V will enhance yield strength, but the baseline is stated to exceed 1200 MPa while the modified-alloy target is only above 1000 MPa; satisfying the stated target could therefore represent a strength decrease.

The predicted elongation is above 10% and density reduction is 5–8%, but the falsification rule only rejects elongation below 5% or density reduction below 2%. Results of 5–10% elongation or 2–5% density reduction would violate the predictions without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
